newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: FEATURE - Nicaraguan papers switch to sex to boost sales.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Nicaraguan papers switch to sex to boost sales.

text.p: Photos of naked women, stories about machete murders and crazed monkeys and headlines like "Sex Between Fatties" are enlivening Nicaragua's once heavily censored newspapers these days.

Experts say more than a new-found freedom of expression in Nicaragua is involved: declining sales have forced too many newspapers to compete for too small a market, and they have turned to sex and violence in a bid to boost circulation.

Managua's four dailies are fighting to survive and making major changes to do so, says one interested observer, Carlos Fernando Chamorro, former publisher of the once-leading daily Barricada and youngest son of President Violeta Chamorro.

On the verge of bankruptcy, Barricada, the voice of the leftwing Sandinista Front, has gone from political analysis to lurid articles with titles such as "Sex Between Fatties" and "Buttocks! What Buttocks!" to gain readers.

Pictures of bra-less women, bare bottoms and bloodied crime victims now decorate the pages of what was the international flagship of the Sandinistas' revolutionary message when they governed from 1979 to 1990. The move to sex and violence has upset some of Barricada's readers among the intelligentsia and feminists.

"I know the world has changed and they have to be commercially viable, but are buttocks on page 1 the way to go? They used to be pro-woman," longtime Barricada reader and feminist Ivana Aguirre grumbled.

Nicaragua's top-selling newspaper, the left-centre El Nuevo Diario, mixes serious news with pictures such as a topless Cindy Crawford and stories of crazed monkeys, machete murders and transvestites trapped in abandoned wells.

Nicaragua's other leading newspaper, the right-leaning La Prensa, censored by both dictator Anastasio Somoza and the Sandinistas who overthrew him, modernised its design and switched to a morning format in December, ending a 70-year run as an afternoon newspaper. Editors said the moves were made to make the paper competitive in the new economic environment.

The new sensationalism is a big change for Nicaragua's newspapers, which were censored by the Sandinista government in the 1980s. "Newspapers were very serious and political in the 1980s. Advertising was banned and it was against the law to use women for commercial purposes," Chamorro said.
But, desperately fighting to survive in the free-wheeling 1990s, newspapers have rediscovered sensationalism and sex.

The changes began in 1990 when Violeta Chamorro toppled the leftist Sandinistas in elections and introduced a market economy and unrestricted press freedom, Guillermo Rothschuh, dean of the communications department at Managua's Universidad Centroamericana, said. "For the first time in the history of the country as a republic, there is an absolute and unrestricted freedom of the press to the extreme that there are no media laws," Rothschuh said.

With the Sandinistas' fall, newspapers no longer received subsidies or cheap paper and ink from the Soviet Union and Cuba. The price of newspapers soared and sales plummeted -- from about 200,000 in 1980 to about 55,000 today.
"In the 1980s newspapers were an inexpensive basic good, but in the 1990s they have become a luxury good. Few people can afford them," Chamorro said.

A boom in private television and radio stations, which now dominate the news market in Nicaragua, has also battered newspaper sales, Rothschuh said. Nicaragua, which had two FM radio stations in 1990, has 93 today, and the number of television stations has grown from two to five, along with the arrival of cable television, he said.

Chamorro said four dailies were not economically viable in Nicaragua and warned that one or more may collapse. Most at risk are Barricada and newcomer La Tribuna, a serious, conservative daily plagued by low circulation.
With sales plummeting from 15,000 in 1990 to 7,000 today, and losing money hand over fist, Barricada laid off 70 employees in December in a desparate gambit to stay afloat.
